rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed ‘waaw of eight’ in the opening of 18:21 is an unfamiliar grammatical category unknown to grammarians; the argument from Paradise's eight gates is unsound.
rows.anchor: إن هذه الواو واو الثمانية واستدل بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exegetes recount that the ruler who sealed the youths in the cave expected them to die there, while two believers recorded their names, lineage, and story on lead and hid the record in a copper chest in the wall.
rows.anchor: أن يسد عليهم باب الكهف ويدعوهم كما هم في الكهف

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: The later righteous ruler who governed the region is called Nadlis; another transmitted form of his name is Bandusis.
rows.anchor: ملك أهل تلك البلاد رجل صالح يقال له ندليس وقيل بندوسيس عن محمد بن إسحاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After generations passed, people divided over resurrection; the righteous king prayed for a sign, and God caused the cave entrance structure to be dismantled, awakened the youths, and exposed their story when one went to seek food.
rows.anchor: وتحزب الناس في ملكه أحزابا منهم من يؤمن بالله ويعلم أن الساعة حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths' long sleep while alive and their awakening demonstrate that the one who can preserve and awaken them can also cause death and resurrection.
rows.anchor: فإن من قدر على أن ينيم جماعة تلك المدة المديدة أحياء ثم يوقظهم قدر أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dispute about resurrection included those who denied it, those who accepted resurrection of souls alone, and those who affirmed resurrection of both souls and bodies.
rows.anchor: فمنهم من أنكره ومنهم من قال يبعث الأرواح دون الأجسام

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: The phrase about disputing their affair is an idiom for what people did in their matter, as in the cited Arabic expression.
rows.anchor: كما يقال ما صنعتم في أمركم عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: An alternative account places the dispute after the ruler and people entered the cave and the youths fell dead; some proposed a tomb-like building, others a mosque at the entrance.
rows.anchor: وهذا التنازع كان منهم بعد العلم بموتهم عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مشركو ذلك الوقت
rows.claim: The command to build a structure is attributed to the polytheists of that time, who proposed concealing the youths from public view behind it.
rows.anchor: أي قال مشركو ذلك الوقت { ابنوا عليهم بنيانا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Their Lord knows best’ can mean that God knows their condition in the disagreement over what should be done with them.
rows.anchor: ربهم أعلم بحالهم فيما تنازعوا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss takes ‘their Lord knows best’ as acknowledging that their Creator, who put them to sleep and raised them, knows their state and how their case stands.
rows.anchor: خالقهم الذي أنامهم وبعثهم أعلم بحالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further gloss says the people were unsure whether the youths remained sleeping and alive or had died; some said they had died, while others said they would not die until the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: أأحياء نيام هم أم أموات فقد قيل إنهم ماتوا

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Those who prevailed over the affair are variously identified as the believing ruler and his companions, the believing guardians of the cave youths, or the town's leaders.
rows.anchor: رؤساء البلد الذين استولوا على أمرهم عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mosque is a place of worship, and the proposal indicates that believers had prevailed in the town; al-Hasan alternatively says it was where the youths would pray if they awoke.
rows.anchor: ودل ذلك على أن الغلبة كانت للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: An alternative explanation is that the mosque was made so the cave youths could pray there if they awoke.
rows.anchor: يصلي فيه أصحاب الكهف إذا استيقظوا عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the youths asked God to restore their former state after learning how long they had slept; God restored it and diverted seekers by making them lose the way to the cave.
rows.anchor: سألوا الله تعالى أن يعيدهم إلى حالتهم الأولى فأعادهم إليها

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: The claim that three or five youths had the dog as fourth or sixth is conjecture without certainty.
rows.anchor: أي قذفا بالظن من غير يقين عن قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Christians from Najran visited the Prophet, Jacobites said three and Nestorians five, while Muslims said seven youths with the dog as the eighth.
rows.anchor: فقالت اليعقوبية منهم: كانوا ثلاثة رابعهم كلبهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Only a few people know the youths' number; another report specifies that the few are people of scripture.
rows.anchor: ما يعلمهم إلا قليل } من الناس عن قتادة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the youths were seven and their dog was eighth, and the author says the likeliest source of his knowledge was the Prophet.
rows.anchor: أنا من ذلك القليل هم سبعة وثامنهم كلبهم

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits Ibn Abbas's list of the seven youths by name: Maksalimina, Tamlīkha, Martūlus, Nīnūnus, Sārīnūnus, Darbūnus, and Kashūṭbūnus; the eighth was the shepherd.
rows.anchor: هم مكسليمنا وتمليخا ومرطولس ونينونس وسارينونس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One interpretation of ‘do not dispute’ allows only debate grounded in the revealed account and proof; Ibn Abbas, Qatada, and Mujahid are named for this view.
rows.anchor: إلا بما أظهرنا لك من أمرهم عن ابن عباس وقتادة ومجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second interpretation permits a public argument that points out conflicting counts and asks the opponents to bring proof, since either claim could be true or false.
rows.anchor: أثبتم عددا وخالفكم غيركم وكلا القولين يحتمل الصدق والكذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation says debate should occur before witnesses so opponents cannot later claim secret prior knowledge and mislead weaker people.
rows.anchor: إلا مراء يشهده الناس ويحضرونه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Prophet is told not to seek information about the youths or their number from scripture scholars; Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada are cited.
rows.anchor: ولا تستفتهم من جهتهم عن ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although addressed to the Prophet, the prohibition is meant for others, since he trusted God's report and should not turn to questioning Jews.
rows.anchor: والخطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم والمراد غيره

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: One reading of the exception supplies an implied verb: do not promise tomorrow unless you say ‘if God wills’; this teaches people to qualify future promises and avoid a lie or broken oath if prevented.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش: وفيه إضمار القول وتقديره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas associates the exception with teaching people to qualify what they report they will do, so an obstacle does not make the report false or an oath broken.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ reads the exception literally as ‘only by God's will’; this fits the surface wording without supplying omitted speech, and can mean that one should promise only acts God wills, namely obedience.
rows.anchor: ومعناه ولا تقل إني أفعل إلا ما يشاء الله ويريده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Farraʾ's reading, the exception does not bar reports about permissible acts, since the prohibition is discouragement rather than a ban: omitting it is not sinful by consensus.
rows.anchor: لأن هذا النهي نهي تنزيه لا نهي تحريم

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi explains the rule by the risk that a person may be prevented by illness, incapacity, or a change of intention; saying ‘if God wills’ avoids a false report because the act did not occur only if God did not will it.
rows.anchor: فلا يسلم خبره من الكذب إلا بالاستثناء الذي ذكره الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When asked about the Cave Companions and Dhu al-Qarnayn, the Prophet promised to answer the next day without making an exception; revelation was delayed for days, troubling him, and this verse then commanded the exception.
rows.anchor: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سئل عن قصة أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: If someone forgets to say ‘if God wills’ and later remembers, one view permits saying it then, even after a day, month, or year; the report is also attributed to the Imams.
rows.anchor: ثم تذكرت فقل إن شاء الله وإن كان بعد يوم أو شهر أو سنة عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says a late exception may earn the reward of making the exception but cannot retroactively change the completed statement or invalidate an oath and its expiation; this best captures Ibn Abbas's intent.
rows.anchor: وهو الأشبه بمراد ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says to remember the exception so long as one has not left the gathering.
rows.anchor: فاذكر الاستثناء ما لم تقم من المجلس عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says to add the exception when one remembers while the speech is still connected; the author calls this the strongest view.
rows.anchor: فاذكر الاستثناء إذا تذكرت ما لم ينقطع الكلام وهو الأوجه

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm takes the command as remembering God by regretting one's categorical assertion after forgetting to make an exception.
rows.anchor: بأن تندم على ما قطعت عليه من الخبر عن الأصم

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: If the phrase begins a new sentence, one interpretation is to remember God by seeking forgiveness when angry.
rows.anchor: واذكر ربك إذا غضبت بالاستغفار ليزول عنك الغضب عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi reads it as turning to God when one forgets something one needs Him to remember.
rows.anchor: واذكر ربك إذا نسيت شيئا بك إليه حاجة بذكره لك عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi understand the command as making up a prayer when it is remembered after being forgotten.
rows.anchor: إذا نسيت صلاة فصلها إذا ذكرتها عن الضحاك والسدي

rows.speaker: السيد المرتضى
rows.claim: Al-Murtaḍā distinguishes an exception that suspends legal force in oaths, divorce, emancipation, contracts, and reports from an exception in sins, where such surrender to God is inappropriate.
rows.anchor: قال السيد الأجل المرتضى قدس الله روحه: اعلم أن للاستثناء الداخل على الكلام

rows.speaker: السيد المرتضى
rows.claim: An exception may also express reliance on divine kindness and facilitation, especially in obedience; if the act does not occur, its absence shows that God did not provide that favor, so the speaker is neither perjured nor false.
rows.anchor: وهذا الوجه يختص بالطاعات

rows.speaker: السيد المرتضى
rows.claim: The verse also covers every act that is not evil, by Muslim consensus on the propriety of making the exception in such acts.
rows.anchor: والآية تتناول كل ما لم يكن قبيحا بدلالة إجماع المسلمين

rows.speaker: السيد المرتضى
rows.claim: For permissible acts, an exception can mean facilitation, ability, release, or continuation in one's current condition; another possible sense is simply declaring dependence on God without changing the statement's truth or legal effect.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو المراد إذا دخل في المباحات

rows.speaker: السيد المرتضى
rows.claim: Al-Murtaḍā answers the opponents of divine justice: if God's willing only obedience made a promise to pay an unfulfilled debt false despite the exception, it would entail a broken oath and expiation contrary to consensus.
rows.anchor: وفي التزلل الحنث خروج من الإجماع انتهى كلامه رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: The hope is that God will grant signs and proofs of prophethood clearer and more guiding than the story of the Cave Companions; the author says God then gave knowledge of earlier messengers and their histories.
rows.anchor: ما يكون أقرب من الرشد وأدل من قصة أصحاب الكهف عن الزجاج

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi alternatively reads the hope as asking God to remind the Prophet of what he forgot, or to give him something more beneficial if the forgotten matter is not recalled.
rows.anchor: وقل إن لم يذكرني الله ذلك الذي نسيت فإنه يذكرني ما هو أنفع لي منه عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most Kufans except ʿĀṣim read ‘three hundred years’ with an annexed genitive plural سنين; the remaining readers use tanwīn on مائة.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل الكوفة غير عاصم ثلاثمائة سنين مضافا والباقون بالتنوين

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan allows the annexed form, though he says Arabs rarely attach ‘hundred’ to سنين; some do so, and the cited poetry supports a plural after the numeral.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الحسن يكون السنين لثلاثمائة

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali argues that the annexed reading is sound because Arabic numerals like three hundred normally take singulars but can take plurals, as shown by poetry and variant formations of مائة.
rows.anchor: ومما يدل على صحة قوله من قال ثلاثمائة سنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With tanwīn on ثلاثمائة, سنين can parse as an explanatory apposition or بدل, or as a specification like ‘ten measures of oil’; al-Zajjaj also permits it as an adjective in meaning, as in the verse of ʿAntara.
rows.anchor: ومن نون ثلاثمائة ففي نصب سنين قولان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir, Rawḥ, Zayd from Yaʿqūb, and Sahl read ولا تشرك with second-person tāʾ in the jussive; the others read ولا يشرك with third-person yāʾ and indicative.
rows.anchor: قرأ ولا تشرك بالتاء مجزوما ابن عامر وروح وزيد عن يعقوب وسهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third-person reading is more widespread and preferable because the preceding context uses third-person forms; its meaning is that no one shares God's judgment.
rows.anchor: والقراءة الأخرى أشيع وأولى لتقدم أسماء الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths stayed in the cave for three hundred years from entry until God raised them and people found them, plus nine more years.
rows.anchor: معناه وأقام أصحاب الكهف من يوم دخلوا الكهف إلى أن بعثهم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘and they added nine’ means nine years; the noun is omitted because the preceding mention of years makes its repetition unnecessary.
rows.anchor: أي تسع سنين إلا أنه استغنى بما تقدم عن إعادة ذكر تفسير التسع

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the three-hundred-year statement is a quotation from the Jews, reasoning from the following instruction to say that God knows how long they stayed.
rows.anchor: وحكي عن قتادة أنه قال قوله: { ولبثوا في كهفهم } الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects treating God's statement as a quotation without decisive evidence; that reading leaves their duration unstated and defeats the passage's proof of God's power.
rows.anchor: بأن أخبار الله لا ينبغي صرفها إلى الحكاية إلا بدليل قاطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The duration has already been given; ‘God knows best’ refutes scripture scholars' disagreement, directing them to God's report rather than their own estimates.
rows.anchor: فخذوا بما أخبر الله تعالى ودعوا قول أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unseen is what lies beyond perception; nothing in the heavens or earth is hidden from God's knowledge, including what creatures cannot perceive.
rows.anchor: لا يغيب عن الله سبحانه شيء لأنه لا يكون بحيث لا يدركه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘How perfectly He sees and hears’ is an exclamation of exaltation: God perceives every visible thing and hears every sound.
rows.anchor: هذا لفظ التعجب ومعناه ما أبصره وأسمعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Jew asked Ali about the youths' duration; Ali answered that the Qur'anic nine years reconcile the difference between lunar years and the solar years in their scripture.
rows.anchor: ذاك بسني الشمسي وهذا بسني القمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one in heaven or earth can protect or support creatures independently of God.
rows.anchor: ليس لأهل السماوات والأرض من دون الله من ناصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On ولا يشرك, one reading means no judge may rule contrary to God's judgment; the alternative imperative means not to associate anyone with God in judgment, while another gloss limits the sense to God's unique knowledge of the unseen.
rows.anchor: فلا يجوز أن يحكم حاكم بغير ما حكم الله تعالى به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to recite what God revealed about the Cave Companions and others, or, in another gloss, to follow and act on the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه اتبع القرآن واعمل به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one can alter God's revealed reports or commands; on the second reading, the phrase means none can change the ruling of His words.
rows.anchor: لا مغير لما أخبر الله به فيه وما أمر به

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Without God and obedience to the Qur'an, a person will find no refuge; other glosses render ملتحد as shelter (Ibn Abbas), recourse (Qatada), or escape and alternative (al-Zajjaj and Abu Muslim).
rows.anchor: ملجأ عن مجاهد. وقيل: حرزا عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads the morning term as بالغدوة, while the other readers have بالغداة; al-Hasan has a noncanonical ولا تعد عينيك and ʿAmr ibn Faʾid reads من أغفلنا قلبه.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر وحده بالغداوة والباقون بالغداة

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali says غدوة is inherently definite like a proper name and normally takes no article, although a dialect may use it as a generic term and admit the article.
rows.anchor: أما غدوة فهو اسم موضوع للتعريف وإذا كان كذلك فلا ينبغي أن تدخل عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The anomalous reading ولا تعد عينيك is connected to turning the eyes away or passing beyond, as in a cited poetic use of تعدي.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله ولا تعد عينيك فإنه منقول من عدت عيناك إذا جاوزتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the reading من أغفلنا قلبه, the phrase may mean one whom God found heedless, supported by the cited use of أغفلت for finding someone in a state.
rows.anchor: قراءة عمرو بن فائد من أغفلنا قلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word فرط means exceeding the truth and going beyond proper limits; سرادق is the surrounding tent or cloth enclosure.
rows.anchor: الفرط التجاوز للحق والخروج عنه

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ruʾba's line about a canopy of glory is cited to attest that سرادق means an enclosing pavilion or canopy.
rows.anchor: سرادق المجد عليك ممدود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word مهل can mean the thick residue of oil, molten copper, or another melted metal; مرتفق is a place to lean on, from leaning on one's elbow, and may also suggest a place of benefit.
rows.anchor: والمهل خثارة الزيت وقيل هو النحاس الذائب

rows.speaker: أبو ذؤيب
rows.claim: Abu Dhuʾayb's verse of the night traveler leaning on an elbow is cited as evidence for مرتفق meaning a place or posture of leaning.
rows.anchor: بات الخلي وبت الليل مرتفقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse was revealed about poor believers Salman, Abu Dharr, Suhayb, ʿAmmar, Khabbab, and others, after wealthy leaders led by ʿUyayna and al-Aqraʿ asked the Prophet to move them because of their smell and wool clothing.
rows.anchor: نزلت الآية الأولى في سلمان وأبي ذر وصهيب وعمار وخباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the command, the Prophet searched for the poor companions, found them remembering God at the back of the mosque, and thanked God for commanding him to stay with people who would share his life and death.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله الذي لم يمتني حتى أمرني أن أصبر نفسي مع رجال من أمتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Keep yourself with them’ means restrain yourself alongside believers who persist in prayer and supplication morning and evening, beginning and ending their days in worship.
rows.anchor: أي احبس نفسك { مع الذين يدعون ربهم بالغداة والعشي }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking God's face means seeking His exaltation and nearness, without ostentation or desire for reputation.
rows.anchor: يريدون تعظيمه والقربة إليه دون الرياء والسمعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was eager for leading polytheists to believe so their followers might follow; he did not desire worldly wealth, but was reproached for sometimes accommodating leaders and told to turn toward poor believers.
rows.anchor: فعوتب بهذه الأية وأمر بالإقبال على فقراء المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of God making a heart heedless means He exposed it to heedlessness; the author compares it with God turning aside those who first deviated.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أن معناه ولا تطع من جعلنا قلبه غافلا عن ذكرنا بتعريضه للغفلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings explain أغفلنا as describing a heart as heedless, finding it heedless, leaving it unmarked with the sign of believers, or abandoning it to its own course after withdrawing support; the last is attributed to al-Hasan.
rows.anchor: ولا تطع من تركنا قلبه خذلناه وخلينا بينه وبين الشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Muqatil and al-Jubbaʾi gloss فرطا as excess or extravagance; al-Akhfash says transgression beyond the limit, while Mujahid and al-Suddi say loss and ruin.
rows.anchor: ضياعا وهلاكا عن مجاهد والسدي

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains the person who neglects the beginning of an affair as one who wastes and destroys it; here the person abandons faith and proof to follow desire.
rows.anchor: ترك الإيمان والاستدلال بآيات الله واتبع الهوى

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: The declaration ‘the truth is from your Lord’ may mean that the revelation is true and came from God rather than from the Prophet himself.
rows.anchor: لم آتكم به من قبل نفسي وإنما أتيتكم به من قبل الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss says the proof has appeared, truth is clear, and doubt has been removed.
rows.anchor: ظهرت الحجة ووضح الحق من ربكم وزالت الشبهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Let whoever wishes believe and whoever wishes disbelieve’ is a threat, not permission: each person chooses what harms or benefits himself, not God.
rows.anchor: هذا وعيد من الله سبحانه وإنذار ولذلك عقبه بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperative form works as a threat because the person threatened is effectively being ordered to bring humiliation on himself.
rows.anchor: وإنما جاز التهديد بلفظ الأمر لأن المهدد كالمأمور بإهانة نفسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The fire's سرادق is a wall of fire surrounding the condemned; Qatada alternatively takes it as the smoke and flame reaching them before the fire, while Abu Muslim treats it as an image of encirclement on every side.
rows.anchor: حائط من نار يحيط بهم عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those suffering thirst and heat who beg for relief are given water like molten metal; Ibn Masʿud identifies it as melted lead, copper, or brass.
rows.anchor: كالرصاص والنحاس والصفر عن ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reported explanations of مهل are oil scum that burns the scalp when approached, oil dregs, pus and blood, liquid at extreme heat, or black water in a wholly black Hell; authorities include Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and al-Dahhak.
rows.anchor: هو القيح والدم عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water scorches and cooks faces as it nears them; it is called relief only because the text pairs it with the word for being given relief.
rows.anchor: وإنما جعل سبحانه ذلك إغاثة لاقترانه بذكر الإغاثة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The fire is a wretched place to lean or gather in; Mujahid derives مرتفق from companionship and assembly.
rows.anchor: ساءت مجتمعا مأخوذ من المرافقة وهي الاجتماع عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and ʿAṭāʾ gloss مرتفق as a lodging or settled abode.
rows.anchor: منزلا ومستقرا عن ابن عباس وعطاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ over لكنّا: Ibn ʿĀmir, Ibn Fulayḥ, al-Barjamī, Yaʿqūb, and Warsh in one form retain the alif in connection and pause; most drop it in connection, and the pause form keeps it save for Qutaybah.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر وابن فليح والبرجمي ويعقوب لكنا بإثبات الألف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj derives لكن from لكن أنا by deleting the hamza and assimilating two nūns; the alif of أنا normally disappears in connection, though some dialects retain it.
rows.anchor: من قرأ لكن بتشديد النون فهو لكن أنا في الأصل

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali disputes that the retained alif is a desirable substitute for the lost hamza: it behaves like a pausal letter and should not be pronounced in connected recitation.
rows.anchor: لا أرى قوله أن إثبات الألف هو الجيد لأنه صار عوضا من الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The anomalous readings لكن أنا and لكن هو الله ربي parse respectively with أنا as the subject of a sentence and هو as a pronoun of the matter or story, as in the quoted verses.
rows.anchor: وقراءة عيسى الثقفي لكن هو الله ربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For retained-alif لكنّا, one grammatical account assimilates the nūn of لكن to the attached pronoun, which then takes a fixed alif; another treats the alif like a pausal extension analogous to a pausal hāʾ.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ لكنا في الوصل فإنه يحتمل أمرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading with هو uses the pronoun of the matter, so the sentence means ‘the matter is: God is my Lord’; the returned pronoun appears in ربي.
rows.anchor: والوجه الآخر أن سيبويه حكى أنه سمع من يقول أعطني أبيضه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vocalized form غورا can be a dialect equivalent of غور and a verbal noun placed where an adjective would normally stand for emphasis.
rows.anchor: وأما من قرأ غورا فيمكن أن يكون غورا لغة في غور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The الياء and التاء readings of ولم يكن له فئة are both acceptable Arabic agreement forms.
rows.anchor: فإن الياء والتاء هنا حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some linguists say ولاية with fatḥa is religious allegiance and kasra is political authority; other usage permits either vowel in either sense.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أهل اللغة الولاية النصر يقال هم أهل ولاية عليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who read الحق in the genitive describe God as the true one or as possessor of truth, by analogy with descriptions such as justice and peace.
rows.anchor: ومن كسر القاف من الحق فجعله من وصف الله تعالى وصفه بالحق

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda reports that Abu ʿAmr considered kasra in الولاية wrong here because the word denotes religious allegiance, while kasra usually marks a craft or office.
rows.anchor: قد حكى أبو عبيدة عن أبي عمرو أن الولاية هنا لحن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda reports that Abu ʿAmr considered kasra in الولاية wrong here because the word denotes religious allegiance, while kasra usually marks a craft or office.
rows.anchor: قد حكى أبو عبيدة عن أبي عمرو أن الولاية هنا لحن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poor believer says his companion should have thanked God on entering the garden: its fruits and crops exist by God's will and power, and God could remove its blessing.
rows.anchor: هلا حين دخلت بستانك فرأيت تلك الثمار والزرع شكرت الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although now poorer in wealth, family, and children, the believer hopes God may give him a better garden in this world or the next.
rows.anchor: إن كنت تراني اليوم فقيرا أقل منك مالا وعشيرة وأولادا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A heavenly حسابان may be a punishment or fire that burns up the garden; another view makes it a reckoning for what the owner earned, and another a missile of hail, stones, or other punishment.
rows.anchor: ويرسل على جنتك عذابا أو نارا من السماء فيحرقها عن ابن عباس وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A صعيد زلق is level earth without plants, so slippery that a foot slides; it would be worse for the owner than the formerly fertile land.
rows.anchor: أرضا مستوية لا نبات عليها تزلق عنها القدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the garden's water becomes غورا, it vanishes deep underground and cannot be recovered; the owner cannot find a substitute for it.
rows.anchor: أي غائرا ذاهبا في باطن غامض منقطعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden's destruction means its trees and palms were ruined completely; the report says God sent fire and the water disappeared.
rows.anchor: أهلك وأحيط العذاب بأشجاره ونخيله فهلكت عن آخرها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Turning the palms over each other expresses grief and regret; Ibn Abbas explains it as striking one hand against the other over the money spent.
rows.anchor: وهو أن يضرب يديه واحدة على الأخرى عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden lying fallen on its trellises means its roof collapsed first and its walls then fell over it; another gloss takes the structures as empty houses with trees gone.
rows.anchor: وذلك أن السقف ينهدم أولا ثم ينهدم الحائط على السقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says the owner regretted his associationism only because his wealth vanished and gained nothing; another says he truly repented of shirk and believed.
rows.anchor: إنه ندم على ما كان منه من الشرك بالله تعالى وآمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trumpet is blown three times: first to cause terror, second to make all in heaven and earth die, and third to raise people from their graves for assembly.
rows.anchor: فالنفخة الأولى نفخة الفزع والثانية نفخة الصعق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All creation is gathered together on one level plain, and Hell is brought into view for the disbelievers to see before entering it.
rows.anchor: حشرنا الخلق يوم القيامة كلهم في صعيد واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers' eyes were veiled from God's reminders because they ignored reflection on God's power, signs, and proofs; hearing the Qur'an weighed heavily on them.
rows.anchor: غفلوا عن الاعتبار بقدرتي الموجب لذكري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking God's servants as protectors means treating them as deities who can save their worshippers from punishment; the referents include Jesus and angels, who are innocent of their worship.
rows.anchor: المراد بالعباد المسيح والملائكة الذين عبدوهم من دون الله وهم براء منهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas offers an alternative rhetorical sense: did disbelievers imagine God would not become angry and punish them for taking deities besides Him? The following verse supports this.
rows.anchor: وأنا لا أغضب لنفسي عليهم ولا أعاقبهم عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj glosses Hell as a prepared lodging for disbelievers, interpreting it as their abode and destination.
rows.anchor: يريد هي مثواهم ومصيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The greatest losers in works are disbelieving Jews and Christians whose efforts in worldly life came to nothing while they thought their actions were virtuous acts of obedience and worship.
rows.anchor: وهم كفار أهل الكتاب اليهود والنصارى

rows.speaker: العياشي
rows.claim: Al-ʿAyyāshī transmits that Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali about the greatest losers: Ali identified scriptural communities who disbelieved and innovated, adding that the Khawarij were not far from them.
rows.anchor: أولئك أهل الكتاب كفروا بربهم وابتدعوا في دينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They rejected God's proofs and the meeting with His recompense, so their works were null because they did them contrary to God's command.
rows.anchor: جحدوا بحجج الله وبيناته ولقاء جزائه في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To say that God will assign them no weight means they have no value, rank, or honor with Him and will be disregarded and punished; Arabic usage treats weight as status and worth.
rows.anchor: أي لا قيمة لهم عندنا ولا كرامة ولا نعتد بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lidd means intense contentiousness; the cited verse and poem illustrate the word and its plural form.
rows.anchor: اللدد شدة الخصومة وفي التنزيل ألد الخصام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rakkz means a faint sound, originally a subtle perceptible trace; the cited verse and poem use it for the sound of hooves detected from afar.
rows.anchor: والركز الصوت الخفي وأصل الركز الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grammatical analysis takes كل as subject, من as its predicate, and the الرحمن phrase as a raised predicate; عبدا is a circumstantial accusative describing the subject of أتى.
rows.anchor: كل مبتدأ ومن في موضع خبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every angel, human, and jinn comes to God as a submissive, owned servant; this establishes that all creatures are God's slaves and includes Jesus, Ezra, and the angels.
rows.anchor: الخلق عبيده خلقهم ورباهم وجرى عليهم حكمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author draws a legal analogy: prophethood and being an owned slave do not coexist, and owning one's child automatically emancipates him.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دلالة على أن النبوة والعبودية لا يجتمعان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows every creature's identities and details, as if He had counted them one by one; each will come alone on Judgment Day, without property, family, or helper.
rows.anchor: علم تفاصيلهم وأعدادهم فكأنه سبحانه عدهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One interpretation makes the promise of love specific to Ali: every believer carries love for him in the heart.
rows.anchor: فما من مؤمن إلا وفي قلبة محبة لعلي ع عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to endure their denials and insults and to praise God in prayer and thanksgiving.
rows.anchor: { فاصبر على ما يقولون } من تكذيبك وأذاهم إياك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Before sunrise’ means the dawn prayer and ‘before sunset’ the afternoon prayer.
rows.anchor: يعني صلاة الفجر { وقبل غروبها } يعني صلاة العصر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes the night hours to mean the whole night prayer; another view specifies the start of night, Maghrib and the later evening prayer.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هي صلاة الليل كله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada and al-Jubbaʾi interpret the day's two ends as the noon prayer, since noon borders both the first and second halves of the day.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول قتادة والجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the command is taken literally rather than as prescribed prayer times, it asks for continuous praise and glorification throughout all hours.
rows.anchor: ومن حمل التسبيح على الظاهر قال أراد بذلك المداومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's satisfaction is explained either as intercession and exalted rank or as all God's promises of worldly victory and honor plus intercession and Paradise in the hereafter.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بجميع ما وعدك الله به من النصر وإعزاز الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʿqūb's Rawḥ and Zayd, as well as Mujahid and Ḥumayd ibn Qays, read خاسر with kasra on the genitive construction; others read خسر with accusative الآخرة.
rows.anchor: قرأ روح وزيد عن يعقوب خاسر الدنيا والآخرة بالجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With خسر, ‘he lost the world and hereafter’ is an appositional restatement of turning back; with خاسر, ‘losing the world and hereafter’ is a circumstantial accusative, illustrated by the cited poem.
rows.anchor: فإن هذه الجملة تكون بدلا من قوله { انقلب على وجهه }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basrans, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Warsh read ثم ليقطع with kasra on the lām; others leave it unvocalized. Ibn ʿĀmir also uses kasra on وليوفوا and وليطوفوا, and Abu Bakr doubles the fāʾ in وليوفوا.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل البصرة وابن عامر وورش ثم ليقطع بكسر اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is inherently kasra; after wāw or fāʾ some readers assimilate it to the preceding letter, while ثم is separate and only analogous to those particles for readers who leave it unvocalized.
rows.anchor: فإن أصل هذه اللام الكسر فإذا دخلها الواو والفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word حرف means edge or side; الاطمئنان is settled confidence, الفتنة here is a trial, الانقلاب is turning back, العشير is a close companion, and النصرة is aid or provision.
rows.anchor: الحرف والطرف والجانب نظائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax of لمن ضره is disputed: one account fronts an emphatic oath lām and supplies an implicit pronoun with يدعو; other analyses construe the phrase as a new subject and predicate or as the object of يدعو.
rows.anchor: اختلف الناس في تفسير هذه اللام فقال البصريون والكوفيون

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj supplies three syntactic possibilities for يدعو لمن ضره: the lām may be a postponed emphatic particle, يدعو may be circumstantial with an implied object, or ذلك may be a relative pronoun whose clause is its object.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: وفيه وجه آخر وهو أن يكون يدعو في معنى يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains that يدعو may mean ‘calls out/says’ or ‘names’; in the latter case the cited Ibn Ahmar verse shows a thing being called by a name.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون يدعو في معنى يسمى

rows.speaker: عنترة
rows.claim: Antara's line in which warriors call to him illustrates يدعو in the sense of calling or addressing someone.
rows.anchor: يدعون عنتر والرماح كأنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The occasion report says some immigrants initially approved Islam only while it brought health, livestock, sons, and prosperity, then rejected it after sickness or hardship; the authority is Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse describes people whose worship is unstable and conditional: comfort reassures them, but a trial sends them back to their former disbelief and causes loss in both lives.
rows.anchor: أي اختبار بجدب وقلة مال { انقلب على وجهه }

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: Worshipping on an edge means weak commitment, like someone standing at an unstable edge, and wavering because a person lacks firm evidence and yields to the smallest unresolved doubt.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن عيسى قال وذلك من اضطرابه في طريق العلم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses worshipping on an edge as worshipping while in doubt.
rows.anchor: وقيل: على حرف أي على شك عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says worship on an edge is worship with the tongue but not the heart, since religion has two parts, tongue and heart.
rows.anchor: فمن اعترف بلسانه ولم يساعده قلبه فهو على حرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person at ease in prosperity becomes secure in worship, but when tested by scarcity and loss turns back to disbelief, losing this world through separation and the hereafter through hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: أي رجع عن دينه إلى الكفر والمعنى انصرف إلى وجهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A preceding report warns Muslims not to return to disbelief and mutual killing; after a man touched his shoulder and the Prophet turned, the text says a verse about seeking refuge was revealed.
rows.anchor: لا ترجعوا بعدي كفارا يضرب بعضكم رقاب بعض

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Hasan explain repelling evil in the best manner as overlooking and forgiving an offender; this came before the command to fight.
rows.anchor: ادفع بالإغضاء والصفح إساءة المسيء عن مجاهد والحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is to refute falsehood with proofs presented gently, clearly, and in a way most likely to be accepted.
rows.anchor: ادفع باطلهم ببيان الحجج على ألطف الوجوه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Prophet seeks refuge from satanic impulses, whispers, and invitations to falsehood and disobedience.
rows.anchor: من دعائهم إلى الباطل والعصيان ومن شرورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request that devils not be present may mean during prayer and Qur'an recitation, or at all times.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه أن يحضروني في الصلاة عند تلاوة القرآن.

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: The plural ‘return me’ may first address God, then turn to the angels with the request to send the dying person back to worldly life.
rows.anchor: استغاثوا أولا بالله ثم رجعوا إلى مسائلة الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation treats the plural as the Arabs' customary honorific form of address; when asked, al-Khalil said he did not know its precise meaning.
rows.anchor: أنه على عادة العرب في تعظيم المخاطب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dying person asks to do good with what he left behind, meaning to pay God's due from his estate, to use his worldly life for good, or to make up neglected prayers, fasting, and acts of worship.
rows.anchor: أؤدي عنها حق الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Sadiq says this plea is made by someone who withheld the obligatory alms and seeks to return to pay it.
rows.anchor: إنه في مانع الزكاة يسأل الرجعة عند الموت

rows.speaker: العياشي
rows.claim: Al-ʿAyyashi transmits that al-Fatḥ ibn Yazid asked al-Riḍā whether God knows counterfactual events; the Imam says the difficult question is answered by God's knowing what disbelievers claim would happen if they returned, though they would repeat their wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: لقد عرف الشيء الذي لم يكن ولا يكون أن لو كان كيف كان يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘No’ rejects return to worldly life; the plea is only a spoken phrase without benefit, as shown by the statement that returned disbelievers would repeat what they had been forbidden.
rows.anchor: لا يرجع إلى الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first explanation makes those in the barzakh separated from the world until the day of resurrection; the dead remain there until they are raised.
rows.anchor: فيه إلى يوم يبعثون عن ابن عباس ومجاهد

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: Ali ibn Isa says barzakh is a period of respite until Judgment Day, identified with the grave; more generally, any division between two things is a barzakh.
rows.anchor: البرزخ الإمهال إلى يوم القيامة وهو القبر

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi infers that at death each person necessarily learns his station with God and whether he belongs among the rewarded or punished.
rows.anchor: أن أحدا لا يموت حتى يعرف منزلته عند الله تعالى اضطرارا

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Barzakh is a barrier between death and resurrection, preventing the dead from returning until the day they are raised.
rows.anchor: { برزخ إلى يوم يبعثون } أي حاجز بين الموت والبعث في يوم القيامة من القبور عن ابن زيد.
